# Can You Sue a Device Maker if Your Doctor Chose the Device?

Yes, you can sue the device maker even if your doctor chose the implant. The doctor's choice does not erase a maker's duty for a defective product. Prescription devices are implants and tools a patient cannot buy alone. A surgeon picks the model, but the maker still designs, tests, labels, and monitors it.
...
## Why the doctor's choice does not block your claim

The Supreme Court of Georgia allowed a claim over a surgeon-implanted spinal plate that later fractured, as described in the court's 2003 decision. The patient did not pick the plate. The maker still faced the suit. That pattern covers hips, knees, mesh, spinal hardware, and cardiac devices.

Your claim targets design, manufacturing, or warnings. It does not accuse your doctor of choosing wrong. You still must link the device to your injury. Keep the implant card, operative report, and revision records together from the start.

## Who must receive the warning?

Under the learned intermediary doctrine, a maker's duty to warn runs to your doctor, not to you. The Supreme Court of Georgia explained that the physician weighs risks for that patient. This means a weak label or missing risk can still support your case. The question is whether the maker warned the doctor fully.

A direct-to-patient warning is usually not required for prescription devices. For causation, the Supreme Court of California in Himes v. Somatics held a plaintiff need not prove the doctor would have refused the device. Proof the doctor would have relayed a stronger warning, and a prudent patient would have declined, can suffice.

But the ceramic joints were defective, the suit alleges, because they didn’t adhere properly to cement used to bond them with the patients’ bones.

Braun and Aesculap in a California court were or will be required to undergo additional surgeries to correct problems with the joints or implant different devices, the suit says.

The process is less rigorous than the FDA’s standard medical device approval process, the suit says.
The lawsuit alleges that the advanced surface joints’ ceramic coating caused moisture to collect between the implants and the bone cement used to connect them to patients’ femurs or tibias.

ultimate.title: Zimmer Biomet Faces Lawsuits Over Smart Knee Implants
ultimate.snippet:
Two California patients are suing Zimmer Biomet and others after receiving smart knee implants they say were placed without informed consent. The cases raise questions about patient choice as connected health devices drive monitoring costs and researchers seek evidence that they improve outcomes.

Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, said he learned about his implant after surgery when Zimmer Biomet contacted him about an app. A company representative later offered to help him set up accessories.
His Persona IQ knee contains a lithium-ion battery, sensors and a transmitter. If Russak authorizes it, the device can send information about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer Biomet.
Russak is suing his doctor, Zimmer Biomet and Canary Medical, which helped develop the implant. His lawsuit alleges he was not offered a chance to decline the knee or opt out of data collection.

Jodi Murphy filed a separate lawsuit in Contra Costa County against Zimmer Biomet, Canary Medical and her doctor. She alleges she received a Persona IQ implant and was registered for Zimmer’s app without specific informed consent.
Murphy’s doctor and her practice denied the allegations. Zimmer’s attorneys said the company did not practice medicine or have a legal duty to obtain consent for treatment provided by her physician.
In Russak’s case, Zimmer and Canary denied the allegations in initial court responses. The doctor has not yet responded to the complaint in court.
Russak said he dropped fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations against his doctor but is pursuing other claims, including lack of informed consent. A hearing in his case is scheduled for December; Murphy’s case has a hearing scheduled for February.
Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick said transmission of recovery data requires authorization when a patient sets up an account. He said the system is designed to support postoperative care.
